extracted.intended_audience: startup founders, early-stage comms and marketing teams
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for early-stage startups on planning and executing media relations, pitching reporters, owning content, and keeping internal stakeholders informed to maximize press impact without a large agency retainer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create your strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a cohesive PR plan before contacting reporters; don’t 'fling yourself into the currents of media without a paddle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure you have key components ready (see specific sub-points). A plan should include target headlines, supporting data/proof points, clear messaging, and a sense for how individual stories fit together so your outreach is coordinated rather than scattershot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write down the headlines you want in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Start by writing the headlines you want all your stories to say, and work backward to craft messaging and evidence to support them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple headline variations for different outlets (e.g., TechCrunch for engineers vs. WSJ for customers). Ask: 'What data do you have that will support that headline? What proof points do you need to acquire and present to the press to convince them of the argument you’re making?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut out all the jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume your audience doesn’t know industry-specific terminology; explain the product/service in familiar words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies if needed. Test a 1–2 sentence description on friends/family/strangers — if they don’t get it (i.e., 'If you can’t explain in a way your parents would understand, that’s a big problem'), revise. Jargon that confuses a reporter merely amplifies confusing messages to your broader audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make relationships that transcend launch
rubrics_metrics.description: Use launches to form lasting relationships with reporters rather than treating coverage as one-off spikes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be grateful, be a resource, offer introductions, host sector dinners or events that give reporters access to experts or unique data. Aim for steady, ongoing interest via trade and niche outlets to compound credibility over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose who to pitch carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Targeting matters: don’t send scattershot press releases to every reporter you can find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a spreadsheet of publications and reporters, and get increasingly selective — the better you target, the higher your chances of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pinpoint your intended audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Start outreach by asking where you want the company to go and who you need to reach to get it there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profile the people who will help you reach goals (e.g., prospective engineers, investors, corporate development execs) and then find what those audiences read and which outlets influence them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick smaller publications and trade outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller or niche trade outlets can be more relevant and easier to place stories in than national press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust that writers at big outlets read trade outlets and often source ideas there. Coverage across many niche outlets compounds and can be as impactful as a single big outlet hit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background check reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Research which journalists are covering relevant stories and capture links to their past work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify reporters’ beats and interests, look for recurring questions or trends in their stories, and note which pieces get the most engagement so you can tailor your pitch to what they care about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research the publication’s readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about the story a publication’s audience wants to read — not just the story you want to tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how a reporter might sell your story to an editor. Give the reporter the facts, figures and arguments they need to make a strong case to cover your story based on what readers want.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft and time your angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern-match your message to what is already interesting or 'hot' in the industry, and explain concisely why the reporter should care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read your industry’s media compulsively to spot trends. Never send a press release with limited context — always explain why you chose this reporter and why it fits their work and audience. Keep outreach clear and not verbose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build authentic, ongoing reporter relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop reporter relationships over time through in-person meetings, warm introductions, and ongoing genuine engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warm intros from investors/board members are vital. Meet reporters at events or for lunch to let them know you as a person. Keep up touch via genuine compliments, sharing relevant items, and multiple touchpoints — build trust rather than transactional asks. Be patient and persistent; expect failure and do not become bitter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warm introductions matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Use people who already have useful relationships with reporters to introduce you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify investors, board members, or advisors who reporters respect and ask them to make intros — those warm intros increase receptivity substantially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet reporters in person when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Face-to-face interactions can drastically increase future coverage opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite reporters to lunch/coffee or start casual conversations at events so they recognize your name in their inbox and feel inclined to open your emails or follow up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep up with reporters regularly
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain ongoing, genuine contact rather than one-off outreach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be inquisitive about their interests, share and comment on their stories, and create multiple touchpoints over time. Authenticity is key — avoid inauthentic flattery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land the dismount on your pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitch in a way that cuts through noise; be strategic and make the reporter’s job easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow specific pitching tactics (differentiate the story, time outreach, prioritize founder outreach when appropriate, provide background materials, and follow up with concise, useful information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate your story
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pitch angles that are already out there; explain why yours is original or a breakout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters seek originality and a different spin. Demonstrate clearly how your angle stands out from existing coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time your approach (when to email and how often)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe unwritten rules about timing and cadence of outreach to maximize receptivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't cold call with a pitch or send repeated 'did you see my last email' messages. Best practices: reach out early in the week (ideally Tuesday), send emails before ~8 a.m. so reporters can bring ideas to morning editorial meetings, and never pitch on Friday afternoon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize founder outreach when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Have founders lead pitches when it will increase reporter interest and access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters often prefer hearing from founders because it signals access to decision-makers; consider founder-sent outreach depending on company stage and the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make it easy for reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide reporters with concise, useful background and follow-up materials so they can quickly produce a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send a brief package before meetings (CEO background, key data, talking points). After meetings, follow up with stats and points mentioned — put facts 'on a silver platter' to increase chance of pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release original data or studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct and publish original research to create newsworthy, reusable content that can generate sustained press hits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie studies to cultural or timely touchpoints (e.g., conferences) and repurpose segments of data whenever relevant news arises. Original, novel data can earn multiple press hits domestically and internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land select speaking opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use speaking engagements to build credibility, meet reporters, and create a 'legitimacy CV.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose events where panel-mates elevate your brand. Speaking makes you ubiquitous to reporters and audiences, and panels can have press in attendance who may cover you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach out to other types of influencers
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify influencers who regularly contact your target audience and secure warm introductions to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Influencers who casually mention your product can bring credibility and inclusion in broader cultural conversations that attract attention from both consumers and press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish your own content (owned media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a content strategy aligned with comms that prioritizes distribution and audience fit over purely promotional materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimize for distribution (SEO is long game but effective). Pick content types suitable for your customers (white papers, webinars, thought leadership, ebooks), make content easily shareable and less salesy if intended to attract press, and maintain a regular cadence — expect content ROI to build over 6–12 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize internal communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep employees consistently informed and engaged; they are potent ambassadors and internal morale is impacted by external press levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use newsletters to share wins and ensure everyone receives the same updates; hold regular Q&A sessions (e.g., weekly 'Heart-to-Hartz') for open dialogue; send empathetic notes during crises. Internal communication should be authentic, consistent, and timely to mobilize employees as advocates and protect morale when press wanes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use newsletters to amplify internal alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribute consistent internal newsletters highlighting updates and wins so employees feel informed and can amplify news externally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a 'brag' section compiling positive indicators such as press hits or milestones and encourage employee participation in sharing wins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold regularly-scheduled open Q&A sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer optional, unfiltered forums for employees to ask leaders anything, building transparency and surfacing culture issues early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, regular sessions (e.g., 30 minutes) that are optional and not recorded can reveal tough questions and help leaders model authenticity and admit unknowns, which builds trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send empathetic internal communications when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge external events and impacts on employees candidly and supportively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders should authentically recognize challenging moments (natural disasters, tragedies, etc.) and outline ways the company can pause and support people; authenticity here is often more impactful than press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for a changing media future by nurturing relationships broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that the media landscape is shifting and double down on building and nurturing relationships with reporters, influencers, readers, and employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target each group specifically, get to know them as people, give them tools to spread your message, and focus on reaching the people who will take action — the channel matters less than the message landing with the right audience.
